location_and_evidence: Methods: Denominators and direct standardisation; S5; standard_weights.csv; independent_output_checks.json
response: We added the direct-standardisation equation and explained how weights are normalised to sum to one within each age domain. Brazil-2014 weights are fixed across years and independently normalised within ≥7, 5–34 and each other domain; each denominator revision uses its corresponding 2014 population. Ages ≥90 form one matching open interval. WHO calculations aggregate five-year rates, combine the three ≥90 weights, and assign three fifths of the 5–9 weight to 7–9 before renormalisation. Allocating that weight assumes a uniform distribution within the band. Independent calculations verified every rate and weight sum; Brazil-standardised and aligned crude rates agree in the standard year.

response: We added Kitagawa's original 1955 reference (doi:10.1080/01621459.1955.10501299), both symmetric equations and the exact identity. All six endpoint pairs were repeated with IBGE 2024. The 2014–2021 composition share is 142.54% under IBGE 2018 and 117.00% under IBGE 2024. A contribution above 100% means that a negative rate component offsets part of the positive composition term. Unrounded identities agree within 1e−12. Independent rounding of each displayed term explains discrepancies in the last digit. The supplement provides age-level contributions and explains the descriptive scope of the decomposition.

location_and_evidence: Abstract; Results: 5–34 and sensitivities; Discussion; S5, S7; Figure S1
response: The abstract now highlights standardisation within 5–34. Corrected crude mortality increases by 0.0358 per 100,000 (19.69%); the Brazil-standardised increase is 0.0328 (18.03%). These revised estimates account for the selection changes and replace the approximate 0.037 in the reference. Removing 2020 gives a positive within-group-standardised slope (p = 0.040). For 2014–2019 the slope is positive but its interval includes zero (p = 0.107); the response and manuscript therefore distinguish the endpoint increase from evidence for an annual trend. The actual years remain the covariate. The WHO sensitivity with IBGE 2018 also includes zero after excluding 2020 (p = 0.055). The supplement reports the same analyses for 7–34, both denominator revisions, Brazil and WHO standards, and all three count families. Differences in study periods and age definitions prevent identification of a historical reversal or change point.

location_and_evidence: Methods: Selection and models; S1, S4, S8; duplicate_pair_audit.md; independent_model_checks.csv
response: Historical exclusions are separated into 56 COVID-related records and one reduced-key removal. Adding U071 excludes one additional 2021 event; the overlap audit shows 18 U071 records in 2020 already excluded and 18 of 19 in 2021 already excluded by the original rule. The primary analysis retains both ambiguous 2018 rows. Their public fields differ in occupation and seven administrative fields; the death-declaration number is unavailable. Matching dates/causes cannot establish identity. Historical-key collapse and retention of all COVID mentions are explicit one-condition sensitivities. The nine age bands, log-link equations, population offset and reference band are specified. Quasi-Poisson intervals use residual-df t critical values; Poisson and negative binomial use normal Wald intervals. Mean-model convergence, dispersion, theta, warnings and errors are retained. Theta iteration-limit warnings are identified explicitly. They prevent a claim of successful dispersion convergence or exact equivalence to Poisson. Independent matrix/IRLS calculations checked all 252 count models.
